Meaning is a semiotic fact, not a thing: 'there is no signatum without signum', so the meaning of a word cannot be inferred from non-linguistic acquaintance with the object without the verbal code, and mere pointing cannot teach whether 'cheese' names this specimen, this box, camembert in general, any food, or an offering.

The meaning of any linguistic sign is its translation into some further, alternative sign in which it is more fully developed (Peirce), so meaning itself is a process of interpretation into other signs.

Jakobson distinguishes three kinds of translation: intralingual translation or rewording (interpreting verbal signs by other signs of the same language), interlingual translation or translation proper (by another language), and intersemiotic translation or transmutation (by a nonverbal sign system).

Synonymy is ordinarily not complete equivalence — 'every celibate is a bachelor, but not every bachelor is a celibate' — so a code-unit can be fully interpreted only by an equivalent combination of code-units (a message), not by a single other word.

The unit of equivalence in translation is the message, not the code-unit: since there is ordinarily no full equivalence between code-units across languages, translation substitutes whole messages for whole messages, recoding two equivalent messages in two different codes ('equivalence in difference' is the cardinal problem of language).

Comparing two languages requires examining their mutual translatability, which is why differential bilingual dictionaries (comparing corresponding units in both intension and extension) and differential bilingual grammars (defining what unifies and differentiates their grammatical concepts) are of high theoretical and practical importance.

Against the dogma of untranslatability, all cognitive experience is conveyable in any language: where a language is deficient, its terminology can be qualified and amplified by loan-words, loan-translations (calques), neologisms, semantic shifts, or circumlocutions (Chukchee renders 'screw' as 'rotating nail'), and no lack of grammatical device makes literal translation of the conceptual information impossible.

Languages differ essentially in what they must convey, not in what they may convey: obligatory grammatical categories force choices the source may leave open (Russian requires verb aspect and gender to translate 'I hired a worker'; number forces 'brother' vs 'brothers'), so a chain of translations can strip a message of content — though the richer the context, the smaller the loss.

In its cognitive function language is minimally dependent on grammar and always admits recoding (translation), but in jest, dream, magic, 'verbal mythology', and poetry above all, grammatical categories carry high semantic import and translation becomes far more entangled.

Grammatical gender is not merely formal but carries mythological and symbolic weight that obstructs translation: Russians personify weekdays and objects by gender, Death is feminine in Russian but masculine in German, and Pasternak's title 'My Sister Life' resists Czech where 'life' is masculine — Constantine the Philosopher's precept is to attend to the cognitive values rather than the words.

Poetry is by definition untranslatable because verbal equations (phonemic similarity sensed as semantic relationship, paronomasia) are a constructive principle of the text; only creative transposition is possible — intralingual, interlingual, or intersemiotic — and rendering sound-based meaning explicit (as in 'traduttore, traditore') forces one to specify translator of what messages and betrayer of what values.

The controlling concept of translation theory in the 1960s-70s is equivalence: translating is seen as communicating the foreign text by a relationship of identity or analogy, and the literature is fundamentally normative — it supplies not only tools to describe translations but standards to evaluate them.

Koller's typology distinguishes four kinds of equivalence: denotative (invariance of content), connotative (similar register, dialect, style), text-normative (usage norms for a text type), and pragmatic (comprehensibility in the receiving culture) — so 'equivalence' is multi-dimensional, not one relation.

A family of binary oppositions — Nida's dynamic/formal, Newmark's communicative/semantic, House's covert/overt, all descended from the ancient sense-for-sense vs word-for-word split — contrasts pragmatic equivalence (so familiar to the receiving culture that it conceals the fact of translation) with formal equivalence (adhering so closely to the foreign text's features that it reveals itself as a translation).

House's refinement is to weigh how much a foreign text depends on its own culture for intelligibility: a peculiarly indigenous text requires an overt translation that is noticeable through supplementary information — expansions, insertions, or annotations.

Equivalence-based theories must reckon with 'shifts' — deviations between foreign and translated texts across linguistic levels (Catford) — which are reframed not as the translator wishing to change the work but as functional fidelity, the translator locating suitable equivalents in the milieu of his own time and society (Popovic).

Levy holds that modern translators intuitively apply a 'minimax strategy' — choosing the solution promising maximum effect for minimum effort, short of violating a readership's linguistic and aesthetic standards — but in average and bad translations shifts tend to generalize and clarify, flattening a work's style into a dry, uninspiring description.

Elaborate typologies of equivalence are ideal schemes rarely realized in practice; they become workable mainly for a narrow range of informative texts (official documents, manuals, news reports) and in institutional settings such as translator training, where forms can be matched directly to communicative functions.

Polysystem theory (Even-Zohar, Toury) treats literary translations as facts of the target system, governed by the norms of a 'polysystem' of forms and canons; translated literature occupies central or peripheral positions and performs innovative or conservatory functions — a minor or young literature may give translation a central, innovating role, a major literature a peripheral, conservative one.

Toury's target orientation transforms equivalence: judging a translation's 'adequacy' to the source is unproductive (shifts always occur, and even identifying a source-text-and-translation pair applies a target norm), so one should instead describe and explain the translation's 'acceptability' in the receiving culture, where shifts constitute a target-norm equivalence at a historical moment.

Holmes's disciplinary map divides translation studies into 'pure' areas (theory and description) and 'applied' areas (such as translator training), importing the scientific model from linguistics and helping constitute translation studies as a discipline.

Steiner's hermeneutic view treats translating as an interpretation that is at once sympathetic and violent, exploitive and ethically restorative, and insists that great translation must carry with it the most precise possible sense of the resistant — of the barriers intact at the heart of understanding — rather than erasing the foreign text's difficulty.

Meschonnic critiques naturalizing translation for mystifying its own appropriation: the maxim that a translation should not seem translated masks an 'annexation' that transposes the dominant ideology under an illusion of transparency, and any translating that forgets its history risks imperialism.

Because no two languages are identical in symbols or their arrangement, there can be no absolute correspondence and hence no fully exact translation — the total impact may be close but there is no identity in detail — and translation always involves interpretation, remaining 'the most direct form of commentary'.
Nida holds that differences among translations are governed by three basic factors: the nature of the message, the purpose(s) of the author and translator, and the type of audience.

Whether content or form takes priority is message-dependent and culturally conditioned: form dominates in acrostic poems while content dominates in the Sermon on the Mount, and though form is usually sacrificed for content, a lyric rendered as prose loses its emotional intensity — yet cultural convention can dictate prose (Homer in English verse seems 'antique and queer', so Rieu chose prose).

The translator's purpose grades the degree of adaptation from informative (a cognitive response) through suggesting behaviour (aiming at full intelligibility so the receptor says 'this is meaningful for us', e.g. rendering 'repentance' as the Shilluk idiom 'spit on the ground', or 'white as snow' as 'white as egret feathers') to imperative (making the action so clear that no one can misunderstand).

Audiences differ both in decoding ability — across four levels (children, new literates, average literate adults, and specialists within their field) — and in interest, so a translation for children cannot equal one for specialists, nor one for pleasure equal one meant for assembling a machine.

Formal equivalence focuses on the message itself in form and content (poetry to poetry, sentence to sentence, concept to concept), constantly comparing the receptor message to the source to judge accuracy; its typifying case is a 'gloss translation' — as literal and meaningful as possible with numerous footnotes — that lets the reader identify with the source-language context (rendering 'holy kiss' literally plus a footnote).

Dynamic equivalence rests on the principle of equivalent effect: rather than matching messages, it makes the relationship between receptor and message substantially the same as that between the original receptors and the message, aiming at complete naturalness of expression and relating the receptor to his own culture without requiring him to grasp the source culture (rendering 'greet one another with a holy kiss' as 'give one another a hearty handshake all around').

Differences between cultures cause more severe problems for the translator than differences in language structure, and paradoxically very closely related languages are dangerous because superficial similarities deceive via 'false friends' (English 'demand' vs French 'demander', English 'ignore' vs Spanish 'ignorar'), so close kinship does not guarantee an easy or good translation.

Prochazka's requirements make three demands of the translator: he must understand the original thematically and stylistically, overcome the differences between the two linguistic structures, and reconstruct the stylistic structures of the original in his translation.

To translate a poem whole is to compose another poem that is faithful to the matter, approximates the form, and has a life of its own — the voice of the translator — yielding a new target-language poem that would not be what it is if it were not translating its source (Mathews, Lattimore).

Nida synthesizes four basic requirements of a good translation: it must make sense, convey the spirit and manner of the original, have a natural and easy form of expression, and produce a response on its readers similar to that produced by the original on its readers.

On the naturalness requirement, the dominant view Nida reports holds that a real translation should not read like a translation at all but should let the reader feel he is looking into the ancient writer's mind, avoiding 'translator's English' — the fluency (domesticating) ideal that later theorists such as Meschonnic and Venuti contest.

When content and form conflict and no happy compromise exists, correspondence in meaning must take priority over correspondence in style (form can be altered more radically than content while remaining equivalent in effect), but the priority must never be applied mechanically — especially in poetry, what is required is a re-creation, not a reproduction, blending matter and manner.

A work's resistance to translation can be a mark of its quality: the most convincing criterion of a work's worth may be that it can only be translated with difficulty, since a text that passes readily into another language without losing its essence arguably has no particular essence (O'Brien, quoting Guerin).

Producing a natural translation is hard precisely because good writing intimately reflects and exploits the total idiomatic capacities and special genius of its language, so the better the original, the harder the translator's task of contending with that exploitation while producing something equivalent in the receptor language.

Judgments of translation quality rest on probabilistic, not deterministic, rules: one cannot call a translation good or bad without weighing a myriad of factors in different ways, so there will always be a variety of valid answers to the question 'Is this a good translation?'

A formal-equivalence (F-E) translation is source-oriented and reveals as much as possible of the original's form and content by reproducing three things: grammatical units (nouns by nouns, phrases and sentences kept intact, punctuation and layout preserved), consistency of word usage (terminological concordance — always rendering a source term by the same receptor term), and meanings in the source context (idioms rendered literally so the reader perceives the source culture).

Formal features that defy equivalent rendering — puns, chiasmus, assonance, acrostics — require marginal notes (roughly equivalent puns like Hebrew ish/isshah rendered as man/woman are rare), so a consistent formal-equivalence translation must be supplemented with notes both to explain lost features and to gloss the formal equivalents that make sense only in the source language or culture.

Describing what kind of translation a text is must be kept separate from evaluating it: strictly formal-equivalence renderings (interlinears, concordant versions, numbered linguist texts) are not categorically ruled out but are often perfectly valid translations for certain messages and certain audiences.

Nida defines a dynamic-equivalence translation as 'the closest natural equivalent to the source-language message', whose three terms point in complementary directions: 'equivalent' toward the source message, 'natural' toward the receptor language, and 'closest' binding the two by the highest degree of approximation — and it must still clearly reflect the source's meaning and intent, not merely be a similar independent message.
For a rendering to be 'natural' it must fit three areas at once: the receptor language and culture as a whole, the context of the particular message, and the receptor-language audience.

Grammatical adaptations are made more readily than lexical ones, because many grammatical changes (word order, verb for noun, noun for pronoun) are dictated by the receptor language's obligatory structures, whereas lexical choices offer numerous alternatives with no obvious rules.

Lexical items fall into three levels of difficulty — terms with ready parallels (river, tree, knife), terms for culturally different objects with similar functions (New Testament 'book' meaning a scroll), and cultural specialties (synagogue, ephah, cherubim) — and for the third class certain foreign associations can rarely be avoided, since no translation bridging a wide cultural gap can eliminate all traces of the foreign setting.

A natural translation is described more easily by what it avoids than by what it states: serious anomalies strike the reader as out of place — crude vulgarities in dignified discourse, misplaced slang or colloquialism, and the over-precise error of spinning a straightforward message into a complicated legal document by trying too hard to be unambiguous.

Anachronism violates the co-suitability of message and context in two ways: using contemporary words that falsify a historically different period (rendering 'demon possessed' as 'mentally distressed') and using old-fashioned language that gives an impression of unreality.

Standards of stylistic acceptability differ radically between languages (what is dignified in Spanish can be 'purple prose' in English), so a translation must incorporate the positive stylistic elements that supply the proper emotional tone — accurately reflecting the author's point of view, including sarcasm and irony, and characterizing each participant by social class, dialect, and individuality.

Fitting the receptor audience requires judging its experience level and decoding capacity, but the translator must also reconstruct how the original audience was competent to respond — New Testament Koine was aimed less at 'the man in the street' than at 'the man in the congregation', who could be expected to understand specialized terms.

A dynamic-equivalence translation inevitably requires formal sacrifices in three areas — special literary forms (poetry demands substituting rhythmic patterns, e.g. free verse for rhymed, or dignified prose for Biblical poetry), semantically exocentric expressions (a literal-meaningless idiom must become endocentric: 'gird up the loins of your mind' to 'get ready in your thinking'; a metaphor may become a simile), and intraorganismic meanings, the emotive and connotative meanings that depend on the whole cultural context and are the least transferable.
Catford defines 'shifts' as departures from formal correspondence in going from source to target language, and distinguishes two major types: level shifts and category shifts.

A level shift renders a source item at one linguistic level by a target equivalent at a different level; because translation requires relationship to the same substance, the only possible level shifts are between grammar and lexis (Russian perfective aspect, marking completion, has no marked English aspectual counterpart and must be rendered lexically, e.g. by 'achieve').

Category shifts (which presuppose some formal correspondence) come in four kinds — structure shifts (the most frequent, e.g. English SPC becoming Gaelic PSCA), class shifts, unit shifts or rank changes (a source group rendered by a target clause), and intra-system shifts; normal 'unbounded' translation sets equivalences at whatever rank fits, whereas 'rank-bound' translation deliberately confines equivalence below the sentence and produces bad translation.

An intra-system shift occurs when source and target have approximately corresponding grammatical systems yet translation selects a non-corresponding term — English singular 'advice' becomes French plural 'des conseils', 'trousers' becomes singular 'le pantalon' — so even matching systems do not guarantee term-for-term equivalence.

Translation equivalence is empirical and probabilistic rather than derivable from formal correspondence: across 6958 cases the French definite article corresponds to English 'the' only 64.6% of the time and the partitive 'du' most often corresponds to zero rather than 'some', which undermines any attempt to set up fixed formal correspondence between the two article systems.

Levy frames translation two ways: teleologically it is a process of communication (imparting the original's knowledge to the foreign reader), and pragmatically, from the translator's working situation, it is a decision process — a series of consecutive moves, as in a game, each imposing a choice among a definable set of alternatives.

Each translation decision has a fixed anatomy: a SITUATION (an abstraction of reality), a definitional instruction that defines the class of possible alternatives (the PARADIGM of possible solutions), and a selective instruction, derived from context, that directs the choice among them — so the alternatives are not equivalent and the choice is context-bound, not random.

Translating is a game with complete information (like chess, not cards): each decision predetermines a number of subsequent moves by creating their context, so choosing among alternatives commits the translator to one of several possible 'games', and different decision-series yield different translation variants whose distance is measured by the number of differing decisions.

A paradigm is not a set of equivalent elements but one ordered by criteria such as stylistic level and connotation (otherwise no choice would be possible); selective instructions progressively narrow it from set to subset until a one-member paradigm is reached, and the choice is governed by both objective factors (the linguistic material) and subjective ones (the structure of the translator's memory and his aesthetic standards).

Obligatory categories of the target language force the translator to make 'surplus decisions' the author never made (Russian lacking a general 'to go' forces a choice among walk/drive/ride/fly); such decisions are necessary or unnecessary and motivated or unmotivated, and the necessary-but-unmotivated surplus decision carries the greatest danger of misinterpretation, reducible only by seeking motivation in ever broader contexts.

The dispersion of possible translation variants tracks the two languages' relative lexical segmentation: the broader the source's semantic segmentation compared to the target's, the greater the divergence of variants, and the finer the source's, the more they converge — a drift that repeated back-and-forth translation (A-B-A-B) makes visible as gradual semantic shifting.

The granularity of equivalence depends on the literary genre as well as the language: in prose 'gooseberry' demands exact one-to-one equivalents, but in verse near-synonyms like 'currant' or 'raspberry' become acceptable equivalents, so a line of verse can be translated in far more ways than a prose segment of the same length.

A source text's breadth of semantic segmentation — its interpretive richness — is why it generates multiple parallel translations: Shakespeare's complex characters admit a wide range of readings and are felt to need several parallel versions, whereas Moliere's minutely segmented, single-meaning elements produce far less dispersion (Harpagon occupies only one segment of Shylock's broader range).

Translation is at once interpretation and creation, involving two kinds of decision — choosing among the source text's possible interpretations (the meaning) and choosing among the target language's possible expressions of that meaning — and in actual practice the translator applies a pessimistic minimax strategy, accepting the solution that promises the most effect for the least effort provided its value stays above a minimum his linguistic and aesthetic standards admit, rather than the theoretically optimal one.

The importance a translator assigns to a stylistic device is a relative value, measurable only against competing values such as linguistic purity: choosing to preserve a stylistic means is an implicit bet on what percentage of readers will feel the language has been violated, a cost/benefit trade-off the translator makes intuitively.

A preserved formal feature communicates only to the subset of readers competent to decode it — whether a reader perceives Sapphic metre or takes it for free verse depends on his knowledge of Greek metrics — so a translator weighing whether to keep such a feature must weigh the likely composition of the audience.

Reiss defines interlingual translation as bilingual mediated communication aiming at a target text functionally equivalent to the source text, in which the translator acts as a secondary sender — translation is therefore secondary communication.

Some change of message is inevitable in translation (a 'communicative difference' present even in monolingual communication, since the receiver brings his own knowledge and expectations): Reiss distinguishes unintentional changes, arising from different language structures and from limits of translating competence, from intentional changes, made when the translation's aims or readership differ from the original's.

When the translation's aims or readership deliberately differ from the original's, the goal shifts from functional equivalence with the source text to adequacy of the target reverbalization to the new 'foreign function' — which is why a translation typology, not just a text typology, is needed.

Because the author's intention gives a text its communicative function, and a text usually has one dominant intention even when it carries several, the translator must first determine the text's type and variety in order to establish that dominant intention before translating.

Functional equivalence decays over time and with context: a source text must be re-translated once the target language has shifted enough that the old version no longer functions (Bible, classics), and a text's own type and function can change historically (Caesar's Commentarii, once an electioneering pamphlet, now reads as an informative historical report; Gulliver's Travels, once operative satire, now a mere adventure tale for the ordinary reader).

Reiss's core typology (from Buhler's three language functions) recognizes three basic text types — informative (communication of content), expressive (artistically organized content), and operative (content with persuasive character) — identifiable through pre-signals such as titles, the medium, and language use (evaluative words and rhetoric signal operative; self-pointing linkage devices signal expressive; their absence signals informative).

A language function qualifies as a text type only if it shapes the construction of whole texts: the phatic and poetic functions do not, because they appear across all three basic types (a holiday postcard is informative-with-phatic, a soccer report can carry poetic language yet stay informative); above the three basic types Reiss adds a multi-medial hyper-type for texts realized together with another sign system (subtitles, song lyrics, staged drama, picture-plus-text).

The translator must establish the text's variety — the super-individual, recurrent patterns of language and structure tied to a recurrent communicative situation, which differ across cultures — and render it with the target language's conventions, so as not to endanger functional equivalence by naively carrying over source conventions (German fairy tales open 'Es war einmal'; death notices and directions-for-use follow language-specific formulas).

Reiss's analysis proceeds top-down through three stages — text type, then text variety, then individual style — with the translator's decisive battle fought at the level of the text individual, where strategy and tactics are directed by type and variety and a detailed semantic, syntactic, and pragmatic analysis is required because form and function are not in a 1:1 relation even within one language.
Reiss's governing thesis is that the text type determines the general method of translating while the text variety demands consideration of the target language's structural and stylistic conventions.

Each text type calls for a distinct translation mode: an informative text is translated according to sense and meaning (making implicit content explicit or vice versa to keep content invariant, e.g. adding 'of the hundred departements'); an expressive text is translated by identification, reproducing the artistic organization even by shifting to a different figure ('last Abencerraje' rendered as 'last knight without fear or reproach'); and an operative text is translated adaptively, adjusting the persuasive mechanism to the new community ('Black is beautiful' cannot be kept for South African buyers).

Because form and function are not in a 1:1 relation, the same source sequence must be rendered differently depending on the text type and variety in which it occurs and the function it must fulfill there (the saying 'Souvent femme varie' is rendered one way as an informative schoolbook citation, another as expressive drama, and another as an operative wine advertisement).

When a text mixes types, the dominant type's translation mode governs all its elements, and conflicts are resolved by a type-specific priority: in an informative text, retention of content takes precedence over reproducing an artistic form; in an expressive text, the artistic organization takes precedence, so content may be changed to preserve it; and in an operative text, the persuasive effect takes precedence, so content or artistic elements may be replaced by others that achieve the intended effect (a Firestone ad's 'Foxes use' becomes 'Pros prefer' to keep both alliteration and positive association).

When the translation's function deliberately differs from the original's, text typology becomes irrelevant to choosing a method and a translation typology replaces it: the criteria are derived not from 'to what end and for whom was the text written?' but from 'to what end and for whom is the text translated?' (as with grammar translations, interlinear versions, and content summaries).

Holmes establishes translation studies as an empirical discipline with two objectives (after Hempel): to describe the phenomena of translating and translations as they manifest in experience, and to establish general principles by which those phenomena can be explained and predicted.

Holmes's map divides pure translation studies into two branches — descriptive translation studies (DTS), which stays closest to the empirical phenomena, and theoretical translation studies (translation theory) — alongside applied translation studies such as translator training.

Descriptive translation studies has three orientations distinguished by focus: product-oriented (describing existing translations, from individual descriptions through comparative analysis of several versions of a text to corpus surveys and eventually a general history of translation), function-oriented (describing a translation's function in the recipient socio-cultural situation — which texts were and were not translated and with what influence — pointing toward a translation sociology), and process-oriented (investigating the 'black box' of the translator's mind, pointing toward a translation psychology).

Theoretical translation studies uses descriptive results plus related disciplines to evolve principles and models that explain and predict; the ultimate aim is a highly formalized general theory, but most theories produced so far are only prolegomena, and many so-called general theories are in fact partial and simultaneously too inclusive (covering non-translations) and too exclusive (shutting out recognized translations).

Partial translation theories — where the real advances occur — come in six kinds, restricted by medium (human vs machine vs mixed; oral/interpreting vs written), by area (language-pair or group; culture-pair or group), by rank (word, sentence, or whole text), by text type (literary, biblical, scientific), by time (contemporary vs cross-temporal), or by problem (equivalence, metaphor, proper names); theories can be restricted in several ways at once, and a body of such partial theories must not be mistaken for a true general theory.

Holmes divides applied translation studies into four areas: translator training (teaching methods, testing, curriculum), translation aids (lexicographical/terminological tools and translation-matching grammars, since ordinary dictionaries and language-acquisition contrastive grammars fall short of translators' needs), translation policy (advising society on what to translate and on the translator's role), and translation criticism (still often low-level and intuitive, but improvable through contact with translation scholarship).

The descriptive, theoretical, and applied branches of translation studies relate dialectically rather than unidirectionally: each supplies materials to and uses the findings of the other two, and one cannot even begin work in one branch without at least an intuitive theoretical hypothesis, so all three must be cultivated for the discipline to flourish.

Steiner models translation as a fourfold hermeneutic motion: initiative trust, aggression (penetration), incorporation (embodiment), and restitution — a structure he argues is inherent in even the rudiments of translation and supersedes the sterile triad of literalism, paraphrase, and free imitation.

The first move, trust, is an a priori leap: all understanding, and translation as its demonstrative statement, begins by granting that 'there is something there' to understand and that the transfer will not be void — a gamble on the coherence and symbolic plenitude of the world, which nonsense, glossolalia, and concrete poetry betray by being lexically non-communicative and hence untranslatable.

The second move, aggression, is incursive and extractive: understanding is an appropriative, invasive act (Heidegger), so the translator, in Jerome's image, brings meaning home captive — decipherment is dissective, leaving the source text 'materially thinner' once its density of otherness is stripped.

The third move, incorporation, brings the imported meaning and form into an already-crowded native semantic field, where it ranges from complete domestication (Luther's Bible) to permanent strangeness (Nabokov's Onegin); no language imports without risk of being transformed, and an immature or disoriented receiving culture may produce mere mimicry or react to expel the foreign, while an individual translator's own creativity can be submerged by the inhaled foreign voice.

The fourth move, restitution, is the ethical crux: because the translator has taken from the source and added to his own language, throwing the whole system off balance, an authentic translation must mediate into exchange and restored parity — the hermeneutic motion is dangerously incomplete without it.

Translation is not only loss but enhancement: the analytic, penetrative process details, illumines, and dignifies its object, magnifying the original's stature and prestige, even though loss is inevitable (Peguy: every such displacement entails a considerable loss without exception); genuine translation seeks to equalize, so that where it falls short it makes the original's autonomous strengths more visible and where it surpasses it reveals the source's unrealized potential.

Steiner redefines fidelity: it is not literalism nor any technical device for rendering the 'spirit' (a hopelessly vague formulation) but the restoration of the balance of forces that the translator's appropriative comprehension disrupted — fidelity is at once ethical and economic, translation being an act of double-entry in which the books must balance.

Even-Zohar argues that translated literature is not a random set of individual texts but a system with its own repertoire, because translated works correlate in how their source texts are selected (selection principles always tied to the target literature's home co-systems) and in the norms and policies they adopt.

The position of translated literature within a literary polysystem is variable, not fixed: it may be central or peripheral, and innovatory (primary) or conservatory (secondary), depending on the specific constellation of the polysystem under study — it does not permanently occupy the periphery.

Translated literature tends to assume a central, innovating position under three conditions (manifestations of one law): when a literature is young and being established, when it is peripheral or weak within a larger group, and at turning points, crises, or literary vacuums; when central it introduces new models, poetic language, and techniques and blurs the line between original and translated writing.

When translated literature occupies a peripheral position it employs secondary models and becomes a major factor of conservatism, adhering to norms the center has rejected — a paradox whereby translation, a vehicle for new ideas, preserves traditional taste and can ossify into a systeme d'antan; empirically the 'normal' position of translated literature tends to be peripheral, and rigid systems like the French keep it extremely so.

The polysystem position governs translation practice, not just status: when translation is central the translator is willing to violate home conventions to build primary models, so the translation is more likely to be adequate (close to the source's dominant textual relations); when peripheral the translator seeks the best ready-made secondary models, producing a greater discrepancy between the equivalence achieved and the adequacy postulated.

What counts as a translated work cannot be fixed a priori or ahistorically: when translation is central the category must extend to semi- and quasi-translations, so translation is not a phenomenon with borders given once and for all but an activity dependent on the relations within a cultural system.

Toury argues that being a translator is playing a social role — fulfilling a function a community allots to the activity in a way deemed appropriate — so acquiring the set of norms for what is suitable, and for manoeuvring among competing constraints, is a prerequisite for becoming a translator within a cultural environment, and cannot be reduced to generating 'translation' utterances.

Socio-cultural constraints on translation lie on a scale between two extremes — general, relatively absolute rules and purely individual idiosyncrasies — with the vast intersubjective middle occupied by norms, themselves a graded continuum (some stronger and rule-like, some weaker and near-idiosyncratic), and constraints shift between these categories over time as whims become norms and norms harden into rules.

Norms translate a community's shared values about what is right, wrong, adequate, and inadequate into performance instructions specifying what is prescribed, forbidden, tolerated, and permitted; they are acquired through socialization, imply sanctions, and serve as criteria for evaluating behaviour, and because they operate only where different behaviours are possible and selection among them is non-random, regularity of behaviour is the main source for studying them.

There is no necessary identity between a norm and any verbal formulation of it: stated norms reflect awareness but also a desire to control and dictate behaviour, so normative formulations tend to be slanted and should be taken with a grain of salt — the actual norms must be reconstructed from regularities of behaviour, not from what practitioners say they do.

Toury's 'initial norm' is the translator's basic choice between subjecting himself to the source text and its norms — the pursuit of an adequate translation, close to the source but liable to clash with target conventions — or to the norms of the target culture, which yields acceptability at the inevitable price of shifts from the source; the priority is logical and explanatory, not chronological.

Shifts from the source text are a true universal of translation, occurring even in the most adequacy-oriented work; the non-random realization of obligatory shifts, and the still more frequent non-obligatory shifts that make up the majority of shifting in any human translation, are themselves norm-governed rather than idiosyncratic.

Toury groups translational norms into preliminary norms (which have logical and chronological precedence) and operational norms: preliminary norms govern translation policy and the directness of translation, while operational norms direct the decisions made during the act of translation itself.

Translation policy is the set of factors governing which text-types or individual texts are imported by translation into a culture at a given time; a policy is said to exist wherever that choice is found to be non-random, and different policies may apply to different subgroups (literary vs non-literary, or different publishing houses).

Directness is a preliminary norm concerning the tolerance for indirect (mediated) translation: whether translating via a mediating language is permitted, prohibited, tolerated, or preferred, from and via which languages, and whether the fact of mediation is marked, ignored, camouflaged, or denied.

Operational norms subdivide into matricial norms — governing the existence and fullness of the target material, its location and distribution, and textual segmentation (hence omissions, additions, relocations) — and textual-linguistic norms, which govern the selection of the linguistic material; segmentation follows no universal pattern but varied traditions, and even sacred-text segmentation is altered to enhance acceptability.

No study of translation should assume that a translated text is representative of the target language or of any overall textual tradition thereof, because translational norms may differ from the norms governing non-translational text production, and their identity must never be taken for granted.

Toury's central thesis is that it is norms that determine the type and extent of equivalence manifested by actual translations, which turns equivalence from an ahistorical, prescriptive concept into a historical one: not a single invariant relation but any relation found to characterize translation under a specified set of circumstances.

Norms have two inherent features that complicate their study: socio-cultural specificity (a norm need not apply across sectors of a society, let alone across cultures, so apparent cross-cultural sameness is coincidence or interference) and basic instability (norms change, often substantially within one's lifetime).

Three competing sets of translational norms typically coexist in a society — the dominant mainstream norms at the centre, the remnants of previous (dated) norms, and the rudiments of new (avant-garde) norms hovering at the periphery — so translation can be trendy, old-fashioned, or progressive, and beginning translators often behave epigonically by following still-existing but dated norms.

Norms are not directly observable; what is available for study is norm-governed behaviour, and more often only its products (even Thinking-Aloud Protocols yield only products), so norms must be reconstructed rather than read off directly.

There are two sources for reconstructing translational norms: textual sources (the translated texts themselves, which are primary products of norm-regulated behaviour and immediate representations of it) and extratextual sources (prescriptive theories and statements by translators, editors, and critics, which are mere by-products, partial and biased toward persuasion); the pronouncements must never be accepted at face value but explicated and confronted with the patterns of actual behaviour.

A translator's behaviour cannot be expected to be fully systematic: decision-making is differently motivated across problem areas and unevenly distributed within one, so consistency is a graded notion between total erraticness and absolute regularity, whose extent should emerge as a conclusion of study rather than be presupposed.

Norms can be modelled distributionally on a return-potential curve with a tripartite gradient — basic (primary) norms that are mandatory for all instances (maximum intensity, minimum latitude), secondary norms or tendencies that are favoured but not mandatory, and merely tolerated behaviour of minimal intensity — so the more frequent a phenomenon, the stronger the norm it reflects, though reconstruction is always relative to the section studied with no automatic upward generalization.

Because norms are always limited to one societal group at a time, moving beyond them to general laws of translational behaviour yields laws that are inherently probabilistic, and in the absence of strict statistical methods research must for now rely on learned intuitions while working toward more systematic methods.

The most common theoretical assumption of 1980s translation theory is the relative autonomy of the translated text: across semiotic, discourse-analytic, and poststructuralist approaches, translation is treated as an independent form of writing, distinct from the foreign text and from texts originally written in the translating language, enacting its own processes of signification.

Frawley's 'third code' rejects equivalence as identity (empirical, biological, or linguistic) on the ground that in communication 'there is information only in difference', so a translation is a code in its own right, setting its own standards and presuppositions even while remaining derivative of the source information and the target parameters.

Blum-Kulka's explicitation hypothesis holds that translation tends always to increase the semantic relations and cohesion among the parts of a text through explicitness, repetition, redundancy, and explanation — a discourse type specific to translating — a tendency toward specification later confirmed by corpus study.

Detecting a translation 'shift' always depends on an interpretive act: no comparison between a foreign text and its translation is unmediated, because it requires a third term or tertium (usually a standard of accuracy, but also a cultural or ideological code) that fixes a meaning in the source and describes the deviation from it.

Holz-Manttari's theory of 'translatorial action' recasts the translator as an expert who designs a product specification in consultation with a client and produces a 'message transmitter' to serve a purpose in the receiving culture, so translation seeks not equivalence with the source but a target text that fulfils the client's needs — foregrounding the translator's professional accountability and a translation ethics.

Lefevere treats translation, criticism, editing, and historiography as forms of 'refraction' or 'rewriting' that carry a work from one literary system into another, determined by patronage, poetics, and ideology, and thereby create canons and traditions in the target culture — giving literary translation the analytical seriousness usually reserved for original composition.

For the 'manipulation' school translation is never an untroubled communication of a foreign text but manipulation; while most work retained an instrumental view of language as communicative, poststructuralism reconceived language as a site of uncontrollable polysemy and translation as interrogative or deconstructive (Derrida) — reducing source meanings while releasing target potentialities that redound unsettlingly on the foreign text.

Poststructuralist theory revives untranslatability in a more corrosive form than Quine's: the problem is located not merely in the incommensurability of cultures but in the inherent indeterminacy of language, so translation is doomed to inadequacy by irreducible differences not only between languages and cultures but within them.

Lewis proposes a 'new axiomatics of fidelity' distinguishing translating that domesticates or familiarizes a message from translating that tampers with usage to match the polyvalencies and expressive stresses of the original — the latter, which he calls 'abusive' fidelity, both resists the constraints of the translating language and interrogates the structures of the foreign text.

Berman grounds a translation ethics in the 'trial of the foreign' (l'epreuve de l'etranger): bad translation is ethnocentric and mystifying, performing under the cloak of transmissibility a systematic negation of the foreignness of the foreign work through largely unconscious 'deforming tendencies', whereas good translation respects the foreign differences by a correspondence that enlarges, amplifies, and enriches the translating language.

Chamberlain shows that a patriarchal model of authority, expressed through gender metaphors recurring in translation theorists since the seventeenth century, has underwritten the subordinate status of translation, and that a feminist attention to gender can both recover forgotten translating women and inform translation sensitive to ideologically coded (feminist or masculinist) writing.

A postcolonial reflection reveals translation as an agent (or subverter) of empire and questions ethnographic 'cultural translation', because asymmetrical tendencies and pressures between the languages of dominant and dominated societies structure the representation of the foreign and can vitiate the anthropological enterprise.

Vermeer's skopos theory frames translation as a variety of purposeful 'translational action': every action has an aim, and the skopos is the technical term for the aim or purpose of a translation, negotiated with the client who commissions it — so a precise specification of aim and mode is essential before the translator can succeed.

In skopos theory the translator is the expert in translational action, responsible for the commissioned result and entitled to decide what role the source text plays, since the decisive factor is the skopos; this dethrones the source text into merely a constituent of the commission rather than the governing authority.

Merely trans-coding or transposing a source text into another language will not produce a serviceable translatum, because the source is bound to the source culture while the translatum is oriented to the target culture, which ultimately defines its adequacy; source and target texts may therefore diverge considerably in both content and goals, and adequacy is measured against the skopos, not against source-fidelity.

Intertextual coherence is the skopos-relative relation between translatum and source text: it holds to the degree the translator judges the source's form and function adequate for the predetermined skopos, so that even an exact syntactic or structural imitation of the source can be a legitimate skopos — provided the translator knows what he is doing and what effect it will have in the target culture.

The skopos has three senses corresponding to the parts of an action: the translation process (its goal), the translation result (the function of the translatum), and the translation mode (its intention), and it may have sub-skopoi; an act with neither goal, function, nor intention is not an action in the technical sense.

Assigning a skopos does not narrow a text to a single reading: one legitimate skopos is precisely to preserve the source text's breadth of interpretation, since a translation realizes something different (not more or less) than the source — it is the realization of one possible interpretation.

Every text production, and hence every translation, is oriented toward a set of addressees, even when that set is indeterminate and fuzzy: producing a comprehensible text implies aiming at a restricted group, which may be envisaged as an addressee-type or inferred indirectly (for example from the range of a commissioning publisher).

Functional constancy between source and target text is the exception rather than the rule, and the neuralgic point where translation practice and theory diverge is precisely where texts are lifted out of their environment for comparison, ignoring their process aspect — dissecting a dead specimen risks findings that are translationally irrelevant.

A skopos is always already present in any translation, whether assimilating or deliberately marked, so the theory requires only that one translate consciously and consistently according to some target-respecting principle without dictating which — and a maximally faithful, literal imitation (trans-coding) is itself one perfectly legitimate skopos, not the absence of one.

A given source text does not have one correct or best translation; because translation is an action it always presupposes and is directed by a skopos, so every translation is carried out according to a commission — explicit or implicit, and possibly set by the translator to himself — that states that skopos.

A translation commission is the instruction to translate and should comprise as much detail as possible on both the goal (the aim of the commission) and the conditions for attaining it (including deadline and fee), explicitly negotiated between client and translator, because the client may have an imprecise or false picture of how the text will be received in the target culture and the translator should offer argued suggestions.

The realizability of a translation commission depends on the circumstances of the target culture, not the source culture (only the source text depends on the source culture); if the discrepancy between the commission and what the target text can bear is too great, no translation is possible, at most a rewritten text.

A translatum is primarily determined by its skopos or commission rather than being ipso facto a faithful imitation of the source, so skopos theory relativizes the once-dominant view that a source should be translated 'as literally as possible' — fidelity is only one possible and legitimate skopos among many.

Skopos theory does not require a translation to adapt to target-culture expectations: adaptation is only one option, and the theory equally accommodates a deliberately marked translation expressing source-culture features by target-culture means, and every hybrid between — the essential thing is to be conscious of the aim of the action.

The value of the skopos concept is threefold: it makes explicit an aim too often denied, it expands the range of possible strategies and releases the translator from the corset of enforced, often meaningless literalness, and it enlarges the translator's accountability — the translation must function so that the given goal is attained — which is the very ethos of the translator.

It is the skopos, not the source text or the source's text variety, that determines the appropriate text variety of the translatum: the same ambiguous will is translated documentarily (with an explanatory note) for a court but instrumentally (finding a target-language ambiguity of similar effect) inside a novel, and Homer's Odyssey has been rendered as a novel because a particular skopos demanded it — so text variety is a consequence of the skopos and secondary to it.

Cataloguing translation 'howlers' leads only to two sterile conclusions — damning all translation and reading originals only, or calling for ever 'better' translators — whereas translations can be used more constructively by studying how they actually mediate a work into another culture, accepting misunderstanding as a fact of literature.

A writer's work gains exposure and influence mainly through refractions: writers and works are always understood against a background, refracted through a certain spectrum, so audiences reach an author through an image created from misunderstandings and misconceptions rather than through direct osmosis of genius.

Refractions — adaptations of a work to a different audience meant to influence how it is read — take the obvious form of translation but also the less obvious forms of criticism, commentary, historiography, teaching, anthologizing, and play production, and these refractions are what establish a writer's reputation and, through anthologies and formal education, conservatively determine which works are canonized.

A systemic approach exposes the assumptions of the Romanticism-based view of literature that cannot admit refraction: the genius and originality of an author who creates ex nihilo, the sacred untouchable text (hence the horror at 'bad' translations), the recoverability of the author's true intentions, and the judging of works on intrinsic merit alone.

The literary system has a regulatory body, patronage, with three components — ideological (literature must not stray too far from a society's other systems), economic (the patron secures the writer's livelihood), and status — usually exerted not directly but through critics; patronage may be undifferentiated (one ideology) or differentiated (competing ideologies, where the profit motive itself can become an ideology).

The literary system also has a poetics, a code with an inventory component (genres, symbols, characters, prototypical situations) and a functional component (how literature may function in society); under undifferentiated patronage one poetics is enforced, while under differentiated patronage competing poetics each field their own critical establishment and the gap between 'high' and 'low' literature widens.

Translation is produced under constraints that go far beyond natural language, and these non-linguistic constraints are often more influential than the semantic ones: translators knowingly naturalize the foreign culture (rendering 'cheese on white bread' as 'cheese on pumpernickel', or substituting Leipzig for Magdeburg) for reasons that have nothing to do with their knowledge of the source language.

A refraction is a compromise between two systems and therefore the perfect indicator of the dominant constraints in both; the gap between the two hierarchies of constraints explains why certain imported works do not 'take' or occupy at best an ambiguous position in the receiving system.

How far a translation defers to the source rather than the target depends on the writer's canonical reputation in the source system: a little-known author is translated largely on the receiving system's terms, whereas a canonized author is translated more on his own terms — according to his own poetics.

The degree to which a foreign writer is accepted into a native system is determined by that system's need for him at a given phase of its evolution: where the need is felt, part of the critical establishment splits off to champion the foreign model.

The deep problem in translating a foreign work is not the dictionary or semantic equivalence but a compromise between two poetics in which the receiving system's poetics dominates: translators of Brecht made explicit what he wanted the audience to piece together, added italics, emotion, and stage directions absent from the German, and padded songs into the register of the Broadway musical.

When a foreign work's poetics is alien to the receiving system, refractors deploy four strategies: accepting the works while dismissing the poetics outright, psychologically dismissing the poetics as rationalized temperament, assimilating the new poetics by translating its concepts into the old poetics' terminology, or explaining the new poetics and showing that the system can accommodate it.

Translations should not be judged in isolation as simply good or bad: a later, more source-faithful version can afford its fidelity only because earlier compromising translations first established a bridgehead for the author and got the critical debate going — a first translation done wholly on the author's own terms, ignoring the receiving poetics, would likely fail outright.

There is no necessary progression toward a single definitive translation, because both the natural language and the politics of the receiving system keep changing and the spectrum through which refractions are made shifts over time; literary systems are stochastic rather than mechanistic, so the categories of a systems approach form an idealized inertial frame that must be applied flexibly to individual cases.

Many translation changes can be accounted for only by ideology, not semantic comprehension: translators play down or omit ideologically charged content, raise loaded words to a nobler register ('field of honor', 'fire and sword'), and remove profanity to satisfy the receiving system's ideological and industry codes.

Economic constraints shape which works are refracted and how: copyright cost drives editors to exclude expensive authors, union rules can force songs to be cut (to avoid a costly 'musical' classification), and commercial safety governs anthology and series contents.

For the great majority of people, only tangentially exposed to literature, the refraction is the original: a text establishes itself inside a system through critical refractions (from learned articles to the blurb), a foreign work enters a new system through translation combined with introductions and notes, and canonization is achieved and maintained through the educational system, with a direct link between college syllabi and publishers' backlists of classics.

Originality in the Romantic sense is an illusion: nothing is ever new, the new being a recombination of old, non-canonized, and imported elements rearranged to suit alternative functional views, so a work is made not in a vacuum of unfettered genius but out of the tension between genius and the constraints it accepts or subverts — and treating a text as original requires isolating it from its tradition at the price of losing its history.

A descriptive systems approach differs from committed critical refractions and poetics-driven translations in that it does not try to steer the reader's concretization of a text in a chosen direction, but instead aims to give the reader the fullest possible set of materials for concretizing the text, which the reader is free to accept or reject.

Even an apparently banal message cannot be translated with a lexicon alone: every message is wrapped in implications and dispositions, so that translating even 'il neige' into 'it's snowing' minimally requires an encyclopedia of culture rather than a dictionary.

Frawley defines translation as recodification — the rendering of coded elements into another code — an essential problem of semiosis and a secondary semiotic process that presupposes the capacity to code: following Eco, copying is verbatim reproduction, transcribing is reducing input into a code (cognizing), and translating is reducing coded input into another code (re-cognizing).

Construing translation as recodification shows it to be both broader than interlingual transfer (language being only one code, so visual codes, religious codes, and logical propositions can also be translated) and independent of identity or synonymy (recodification occurs and is valid whether or not an element of one code is synonymous with its correlate in another, since code-crossing plainly occurs while the identity question remains unsolved).

Frawley models translation with two codes — the matrix code of origin, which supplies the information to be recodified, and the target code, which supplies the parameters for rerendering — and stresses that translation is not one-way but a perpetual reflexive shuffling in which the matrix information accommodates the target parameters as much as the parameters accommodate the information.

The three arguments for identity across codes all fail: the referential argument (meaning as reference to constant phenomena) fails because there is no meaning apart from the code — 'table' signifies through its systematic relations within English, not through the wooden object; the conceptual/biological argument fails for lack of any grammar-cognition correlation; and the linguistic-universals argument yields only contingent, merely-sufficient, or trivially-necessary universals that cannot ground useful identity.

Using point-by-point identity in translation turns it into copying, mimicry, or transliteration, because correlating a semiotic element across codes fails to capture the surrounding code structure — a sentential adverb is acceptable in Spanish yet despised in written English, so an element enters different structural relations in each code.

Identity is useless for translation because universal grammar and its identities are matters of competence and are absolute, whereas translation is a matter of performance and is probabilistic; the interest of translation stems precisely from the uncertainty caused by the inevitable structural mismatch of codes, so where whole structures are identical the recoding is academic and not even worthy of the name translation.

The semantic 'essence' of a text is only a small fraction of the total information a source code carries (phonological, morphological, syntactic, and pragmatic information as well), so any interlingual translation that seeks to transfer only the semantics has lost before it has begun.

The translation is a third code that arises from the bilateral consideration of the matrix and target codes: with a dual lineage it emerges as a code in its own right, setting its own standards and entailments and dictating its own logic, and this is both the bane and the breath of life of translation because there is information only in difference — without the individuated third code the translation would carry no information at all.

The target code functions as a virtual text — a set of parameters and well-formedness constraints never realized in itself — that binds the source information rather than supplying exact correlated elements, so literary translation is the mediation between a tangible source text and a virtual target text.

The third code establishes its own semantic necessities, accountable to neither the matrix nor the target code, which can legitimately override standard lexical fidelity: Tarn renders 'novia sumergida' as 'bride in her veil of sea' rather than 'submerged bride' and 'el alto vacio' as 'the rare height' rather than 'the empty height', and the text does not suffer from these breaches of fidelity.

When a source text contains irreducible ambiguity — such as poetic compression or non-recoverable syntactic deletion that leaves several equally plausible deep structures — the translator's disambiguating choice does not invalidate the translation, because the source was multiply ambiguous and the target could accommodate any of the readings; it is a legitimate matter of performance.

Frawley argues that a respectable theory of translation must abandon the notions of good, bad, and fidelity as it abandoned identity and 'preservation of meaning' — since strict fidelity to the source produces awkward rather than interesting texts, and would make machines the 'best' translators — and can at most classify a translation as a moderate innovation (a close translation adhering to the matrix, or a free translation adhering to the target, both yielding only moderate new information) or a radical innovation that breaks away from both codes and carries the most semiotic information.

Translation is an act of sign-production, not sign-translation: the new code is a semiotic unit in its own right that signifies by its own individuation, so it is not that a sign becomes translated or that a universal significance is disembodied and reincarnated — recodification produces a genuinely new sign.

A translator (here Lewis translating his own French) should aim at more than a stilted transfer of meanings: he should make the text 'work' in the target language with the texture of a piece written for that audience, adapting even the emphasis — e.g. foregrounding practical processes and results for an Anglophone readership rather than a more theoretical excursus.

Contrastive discourse analysis of French and English (Guillemin-Flescher, via translations of Madame Bovary) reveals systematic differences along two structural orders — modes of enunciation (observation vs commentary, direct vs indirect discourse) and forms of contextual binding (reperage) — showing that English favors actualization (concrete occurrence in context), direct constative reference, a tighter network of internal linkages, and consistency of related terms, so that English calls for more explicit, precise, concrete, and cohesive determinations than French.

The deep problem of translation is not merely imprecise lexical correspondence or the absence of a prescriptive theory, but that the target language imposes its own set of discursive relations and its own construction of reality: when English rearticulates a French utterance it puts an interpretation built into English on it and simply cannot let the original say what it says in French.

The difference that arises from the dissimilarity of languages is the difference always already in translation — the very ground, raison d'etre, and principle of translation, which cannot be overcome; it may be glossed over but is never totally suppressed.

A good translation faces a contradictory demand and is therefore always already a double interpretation: it must be faithful both to the language and message of the original and to the message-orienting cast of its own language, and because these two interpretations are mutually exclusive, every translation is consigned to a degree of inadequacy.

A translator who is also the author of the original has an option unavailable to the translator of another's text — shifting at will between conventional translation that must violate the original and commentary that compensates for its inadequacy — so for the ordinary translator, deprived of the commentarial option, the central question is whether and how anything can be done to preserve the tenor, texture, and tangents of the source that the target language would otherwise override.

A 'good' translation must sometimes commit abuses (Derrida): an abusive rendering such as translating German Entziehung by French retrait functions not as equivalence but as a factor in an economy of translation — a process of gain as well as loss conceived quantitatively rather than qualitatively — whose controlled disruption unpacks and disseminates meaning and thereby justifies the translator's work.

Lewis's axiology of translation poses two risks: the risk to overcome is weak, servile translation that privileges the 'us-system' (the usual, the useful, common usage) and so domesticates the message at the expense of whatever might force language and thought; the risk to assume is strong, forceful translation that values experimentation, tampers with usage, and seeks to match the polyvalencies and expressive stresses of the original by producing its own.

Conventional translation of expository writing tends to privilege the capture of signifieds — giving primacy to message, content, or concept over language texture — so it works by substitution and re-presentation while subordinating or losing the order of syntax and metonymy in which the original's signifiers are linked and its poetic 'textual work' is carried on.

Lewis proposes a new axiomatics of fidelity that demands fidelity to far more than semantic substance — to the chain of signifiers, to syntactic processes, to discursive structures, and to the modalities of expression and rhetorical strategies — so the translator's problem shifts from avoiding the inevitable failures to compensating for losses and renewing the signifying energy a translation would otherwise diffuse.

An abusive move in translation must not be directed at just any element but must bear upon a key operator or decisive textual knot — a point that is forced or stands out as a cluster of textual energy (a word, a turn of phrase, a formulation) that resists the preponderant values of the usual and useful.

Abusive translation foreignizes in two directions at once: it forces the linguistic and conceptual system of the target language from within, and it directs a critical thrust back at the source text so that, far from domesticating the original, it renders the original still more foreign to itself.

Texts whose strategy is grounded in the capacity of discourse to say and do many things at once and to leave some relations indeterminate (operators of undecidability, as in Derrida) are exceptionally resistant to translation, so philosophy and linguistic theory must reckon with untranslatability rather than defensively dismiss it.

Translation is essayistic in the strong sense: because the combinations of use and abuse across the language of the original, the language of the translation, and the space between are elusive and logistically impracticable to program, the integration achieved escapes systematic reflection and emerges in an experimental order of discovery where success depends on trial, error, and chance as well as on language's paraphrastic capacities.

Lewis's abusive-fidelity evaluation scheme judges a translation by three moves — concentrate attention on the moments of density and intensity where the play of concepts is affected by the disruptive power of language, insist on the transformations the translation makes at the syntactic and discursive levels and not just the semantic, and ask whether the translation articulates its own textual effects that are tellingly abusive with respect to the original — applied through close line-by-line and word-by-word comparison.

Paratextual and typographic changes are subtractive and flatten the original: dropping the italics that set off terms, adding quotation marks the source does not have, and inserting unmarked translator's notes all soften and diminish a writer who is careful about textual geography.

A translation must preserve the source text's own handling of foreign and translated words (bracketed Greek or German originals, italicized foreign terms); dropping them and making do with just the target word reduces the attention to translation that the original deliberately sustains.

Morphological simplification trivializes technical concepts: suppressing a conceptually loaded suffix (rendering 'metaphorique' as 'metaphor' rather than 'metaphorics', or 'philosopheme' as 'an element of philosophy') strips a term of its special value as a basic unit in a structured system.

Substituting a semantic neighbor for a key term when a more literal alternative is available — translating 'effect' as 'phenomenon', 'valeur' as 'notion', 'articulation' as 'joint' — need not radically change a statement's meaning but occasions an unnecessary loss of precision, especially damaging for an author's strategic vocabulary.

Phrase-level changes can set aside a key concept or reverse an argument: converting 'metaphoricite par analogie' to 'analogy producing metaphor' discards the term for metaphor's general status, and rendering a single 'condition of impossibility' as 'the conditions which make it in principle impossible' misstates an argument built on one disabling principle.

Assimilating a text to the target language's discourse norms alters the author's stance: tightening loosely separated sentences with added conjunctions and adversatives, converting a conditional to an assertive form, expanding deliberately elliptical utterances into full subject-verb sentences, and introducing a participial agent absent in the source all give a theoretical text a falsely immediate, practical tenor.

Repetition, parallelism, and a key term's polysemy carry argumentative structure rather than mere elegance, so dropping them drains the argument: omitting a repeated limitative adverb ('seul... seul... seul') destroys the parallelism that marks propositions as refinements, collapsing a polysemous conceptual shifter (Derrida's 'tour', spanning turn, revolution, trick, twist, and linked to retour and detour) into a single sense loses its articulatory power, and suppressing one load-bearing word (such as 'history') can gut the point.

Some texts perform their own thesis — enacting in their rhetoric and syntax the very processes they argue about — so a translation that renders only the message and lets the performative dimension lapse does not merely miss a nuance but saps the strength of the thesis by severing its enactment from its statement.

Translation tends to recuperate a source's disruptive force back under the control of a reigning target-language interpretation (domestication by the natural language), a recuperation a strong translation must run and overcome; it can never be wholly thwarted, so the practical question is how far the recuperative effects can be controlled and the original's resistance remobilized in the translating language.

Weak, entropic translations partly reflect a time factor: strong translation derives from insightful reading, which derives from a familiarity gained only over time, so the closer a translation of a difficult monumental text is to the original's date of publication, the more likely it is to be unduly deficient.

Berman frames translation as the trial of the foreign in a double sense: it establishes a relation between the Self-Same and the Foreign by aiming to open the foreign work to us in its utter foreignness (which classic translations tend to attenuate or cancel), and it is a trial for the Foreign as well, since the work is uprooted from its language-ground in an exile that can reveal its most original, most deeply buried kernel.

For Hollderlin, and for Berman, translating means liberating the violence repressed in a work through intensifications in the translating language that accentuate its strangeness — and paradoxically this accentuation of foreignness is the only way of giving the reader genuine access to the work.

Foucault distinguishes two kinds of translation that map to the literary/non-literary split: one in which something (meaning, aesthetic value) must remain identical and is given passage 'from like to same' (non-literary semantic transfer of texts instrumentally related to their language), and one that hurls one language against another — using the original as a projectile and the translating language as a target to derail it — which literary works, bound to their language, demand.

The proper aim of the translating act is ethical — to receive the Foreign as Foreign — but in the literary domain this aim has from time immemorial been skewed and perverted, so that translation becomes the negation, acclimation, and naturalization of the foreign rather than its trial.

Berman's 'analytic of translation' is the examination of the system of textual deformation operating in every translation, analytic in the Cartesian sense (a detailed analysis of the deforming forces) and the psychoanalytic sense (the system is largely unconscious, part of the translator's being and desire, so mere awareness does not free the translator — the practice must submit to analysis); pairing this negative analytic with a positive counterpart of deformation-limiting operations yields a critique of translations that is neither simply descriptive nor simply normative.

The 'shapelessness' and apparent 'bad writing' of great prose — the lack of control seen in Rabelais, Cervantes, and Dostoevsky, where the novel is a consumer rather than a producer of style — is not a flaw but the richness of its polylingualism, its gathering of the many coexisting languages of a community into one work.

The principal problem of translating the novel is to respect its shapeless polylogic and avoid an arbitrary homogenization (as poetry's is to respect polysemy); because the novel is deemed a lower form, its deformations are more accepted and often unperceived — it is easy to see a Hollderlin poem massacred but hard to see what was done to a novel by Kafka or Faulkner, especially if the translation seems 'good', so the deforming system operates in complete tranquillity.

Berman names twelve deforming tendencies that form a systematic whole and bear on all translating in the western tradition: rationalization, clarification, expansion, ennoblement and popularization, qualitative impoverishment, quantitative impoverishment, the destruction of rhythms, the destruction of underlying networks of signification, the destruction of linguistic patternings, the destruction of vernacular networks or their exoticization, the destruction of expressions and idioms, and the effacement of the superimposition of languages.
